Core¶

The generic machinery: the post templates, the visits and the cursor, the concepts, and the structural operations that belong to no particular automaton class. Nothing here depends on a concrete relation: no header in core/ includes the one this library ships, and its comments name it only as an example. A third party building their own relation therefore compiles all of this without inheriting mata::Delta. tests/core/core-only.cc holds core/ to that, and builds an automaton from core/ alone over keys and states that are not mata::Symbol and mata::State.

That one lives in The shipped relation, and Nondeterministic Finite automata and Nondeterministic Finite Transducers re-export it through their own seams, so mata::nfa::Delta and mata::Delta currently name the same type.

Traits for relation and post types.

A relation is described by three traits: what a target denotes, where the reserved keys begin, and how deep a chain of posts is.

template<typename T>
struct TargetTraits¶
#include <traits.hh>

A traits specifying which state a target denotes.

A target is whatever the innermost post stores: a state, or a state with a payload. The structural algorithms need two things from it: state_of(target) to know the state it denotes, and with_state(target, state) to rebuild a target with a new state when reverting, renumbering or trimming. Both are the identity for a bare state.

The default covers only a bare state, an integral type. Any other target has to specialise this, and one that does not is stopped here, rather than being taken for a state and failing deep inside an algorithm that indexes by it.

The order of the targets has to follow their states: renaming the states by a strictly increasing map, as trimming does, must not reorder the targets. Any order comparing the state by <, wherever it comes in the comparison, does so, which includes every defaulted <=>. An order that is not monotone in the state, such as even states before odd ones, does not, and trimming would leave its target sets unsorted.

An example of specialization for a target with MyPayload is: 

template <> struct mata::TargetTraits<MyPayload> {
using State = mata::State;
static State state_of(const MyPayload& t) { return t.state; }
static MyPayload with_state(const MyPayload& t, State s) { return {s, t.payload}; }
};

template<typename K, K MinEpsilon = std::numeric_limits<K>::max(), K MaxOrdinary = internal::default_max_ordinary<K>(MinEpsilon), bool EpsilonIsGreatest = internal::default_epsilon_is_greatest<K>(MinEpsilon)>
struct ReservedKeys¶
#include <traits.hh>

The structure defines where the ordinary keys stop and the reserved tail begins.

The key order splits into three regions:

  • ordinary, up to and including max_ordinary

  • reserved but not epsilon, above max_ordinary and below min_epsilon

  • epsilon, from min_epsilon upwards

The middle region is empty by default, since MaxOrdinary defaults to one below MinEpsilon. Widening the reserved tail opens it, which is how a key can be reserved.

Template Parameters:

  • K – The key type.

  • MinEpsilon – The smallest epsilon key: every key at or above it is an epsilon. Defaults to the largest value. A non-integral key has no default and must be spelled explicitly.

  • MaxOrdinary – The largest key that is not reserved. Defaults to one below MinEpsilon. Can be defined explicitly to a smaller value to open the reserved-but-not-epsilon region. A non-integral key has no default and must be spelled explicitly.

  • EpsilonIsGreatest – Whether no key sorts above MinEpsilon. Defaults to true only for an integral key whose MinEpsilon is its largest value.

template<typename P>
struct SymbolTransitionTraits¶
#include <transition.hh>

Traits for a transition type: how to build one and how to take it apart.

A traits names a Type and builds transition with make(source, keys..., target), one key per post. The type itself owes a static parts(), which is what lets the hash, the formatter and the transition-shaped members of DeltaBase work without knowing the type.

Two are shipped. SymbolTransitionTraits yields the {source, symbol, target} triple and is the default at arity 1. KeyedTransitionTraits yields {source, keys, target} with the keys as a tuple and is the default above arity 1. DefaultTransitionTraits picks between them.

A module that wants its own field names writes a traits and passes it as the second argument of DeltaBase. Nothing is specialised, so two modules over the same chain can name their fields differently without touching each other: 

struct Transition {
State source{}; Symbol input{}, output{}; State target{};
bool operator==(const Transition&) const = default;
static auto parts(const Transition& t) noexcept {
using utils::ArgOf;
return std::tuple<ArgOf<State>, ArgOf<Symbol>, ArgOf<Symbol>, ArgOf<State>>{
            t.source, t.input, t.output, t.target};
    }
};
struct TransitionTraits {
using Type = Transition;
static Type make(State s, Symbol in, Symbol out, State t) { return {s, in, out, t}; }
};
// Right after the type, before anything hashes or formats one:
template <> struct std::hash<Transition> {
size_t operator()(const Transition& t) const noexcept { return mata::posts::hash_of(t); }
};
template <> struct std::formatter<Transition> { ... return mata::posts::format_parts(ctx.out(), t); ... };

class Delta : public mata::posts::DeltaBase<StatePost, TransitionTraits> { ... };

template<typename D>
class DeltaTransitions
#include <transition.hh>

Iterator over the transitions of a relation.

A non-owning view: it must not outlive the relation, and changing the relation invalidates its iterators. Transitions come by ascending source, then in the order of the relation’s CursorType. Each is built on the fly with TransitionTraits::make, so *it refers to a value held by the iterator and is invalidated by ++it.

The visits over a chain of posts: reading, writing and rebuilding at any nesting depth.

Free functions over a post P, each recursing on mata::arity_of until it reaches the targets. They are what mata::posts::Post, mata::posts::DeltaBase and mata::AutomatonBase share, so the depth is handled once, here, and not again in every class that holds a post.

template<typename P, typename Fn>
void visit_targets(const P &post, Fn &&fn)¶

Apply fn to every target under post, at any nesting depth.

.

Note

if constexpr on key_arity turns the recursion into nested loops (same as a caller would write by hand), making this depth-generic visit free: measured at 0.99-1.01x of hand-written loops at every arity from 1 to 9. Fn is a template parameter and never a std::function: routing the same visit through one would cost 1.08x to 2.18x.

Parameters:

  • post – The post to visit. mata::arity_of is used to recurse down to the innermost post.

  • fn – The callable to apply to each target. It must accept a single argument of type target_of

void visit_moves(const P &post, Fn &&fn, const Keys&... keys)¶

Apply fn to every move under post, as fn(keys..., target).

.

Note

template<typename P>
bool posts_equal(const P &a, const P &b)¶

Returns whether a and b structurally equal, including every target under them.

Note

This is a deep comparison, not a shallow one. Standard operator== on a post compares only the keys of its entries, so it ignores every difference in the targets. To properly compare two posts, you need to use this function.

Parameters:

  • a – The first post to compare.

  • b – The second post to compare.

Returns:

true if a and b are structurally equal, false otherwise.

template<typename P, typename Fn>
P renumbered(const P &post, Fn &&rename)¶

Rebuild post with every target renamed by function rename.

The targets stay sorted and duplicate-free for any rename. A strictly increasing one costs one comparison per target. One that merges states or reorders them falls back to an ordered insert.

Parameters:

  • post – The post to rebuild. mata::arity_of is used to recurse down to the innermost post.

  • rename – The callable to apply to each target’s state. It must accept a single argument of type state_of<target_of<P>> and return a new state of the same type.

Returns:

A new post with the same structure as post, but with every target’s state renamed by rename.

template<typename P, typename Renaming>
P defragmented(const P &post, const BoolVector &is_staying, const Renaming &renaming)¶

Rebuild post keeping only the targets is_staying admits, and renaming their states.

Parameters:

  • post – The post to rebuild. mata::arity_of is used to recurse down to the innermost post.

  • is_staying – Indexed by old state, true for a state that stays. It must cover the state of every target in post.

  • renaming – Indexed by old state, the new state of a staying one. It must cover every staying state of a target in post.

Returns:

A new post with the same structure as post, but with only the targets whose states are staying, and with their states renamed according to renaming.

template<typename P, typename Renaming>
inline void defragment_in_place(P &post, const BoolVector &is_staying, const Renaming &renaming)¶

Keep in post only the targets is_staying admits, renaming their states, in place.

The renaming is monotone on the staying states, so the sets stay sorted, given a target order that follows the states (see mata::TargetTraits). Entries left without targets are erased.

Parameters:

  • post – The post to filter. mata::arity_of is used to recurse down to the innermost post.

  • renaming – Indexed by old state, the new state of a staying one. It must cover every staying state of a target in post.

template<typename P>
class PostMoves
#include <moves.hh>

The moves of a post as Move instances: every (symbol, target) pair, or a range of them.

Available only at key_arity 1, since a Move holds a single key. Above that, use for_each_move().

Template Parameters:

P – The post visited.

Pre:

No symbol post in the range is without targets: for speed, the iterator does not skip one. Mata’s own writes keep a post so, as remove() and defragment() erase the symbol posts they empty. A symbol post created empty through mutable_state_post() has to get its targets before its moves are iterated. for_each_move() and the successor cursors have no such precondition.

Definition of one post of a relation, and one entry of it.

Post structure¶

A relation is DeltaBase indexed by source state, over a chain of posts ending in a set of targets. There is one post per key, so a relation with n keys is n posts deep: 

DeltaBase -> Post -> Post -> ... -> Targets
              key 0   key 1         (a state, or a state with a payload)
A Post is an ordered map from one key to the post nested under it. Iterating over one yields its PostEntry objects, each one key paired with the post beneath it. The same two classes make up every step of the chain. mata::StatePost and mata::SymbolPost are aliases for the depth-2 instantiation. PostChain spells a chain outermost key first.

Sortedness¶

Every post is sorted by key, and the innermost one by target. Lookups binary-search on it, and Post::first_epsilon_it() scans backwards relying on that order alone: a sorted range splits at any threshold into “below” then “at or above”. A post that does not maintain the order still compiles, and silently returns wrong iterators. The order may be broken temporarily: push_back and emplace_back append without restoring it, which is faster when building from unordered input. It has to be then restored by sorting before any lookup, iteration order or comparison is relied upon. A post advertises that it maintains the invariant with sorted_by_key / sorted_by_target and exposes is_sorted().

template<typename P, typename TT = DefaultTransitionTraits<P>>
class DeltaBase : public mata::posts::KeyedAccess<DeltaBase<P, DefaultTransitionTraits<P>>, P>
#include <delta.hh>

The generic transition relation: a vector of posts indexed by source state.

A vector of posts indexed by source state, over a chain of posts ending in a set of targets. The depth is deduced from P as key_arity. Posts are named by key index, not by container count: Key<0> is the topmost symbol, and PostAt<key_arity> is the innermost post.

See also

mata::posts::DefaultTransitionTraits.

See also

mata::DeltaLike.

Template Parameters:

  • P – The post reached from one source state, itself parameterised down to the targets.

  • TT – What one transition of this relation looks like and how to build one: a traits with a Type and a make(). Defaults to the symbol-named triple at arity 1 and to the tuple-keyed transition above it.

Keys on the transitions

Which outermost keys are in use. They ask nothing of a key beyond the ordering the posts already rely on, so a relation keyed by an interval or a weight has them too; what those keys stand for is that relation’s business. Protected for the same reason: a relation re-exports the ones it wants under the names that fit its keys, with a using-declaration or a forwarder. mata::Delta does the latter, as symbols, since for the shipped relation a key is one.

The three variants indexed by the key’s value need an unsigned integer for it.

Get constant reference to the state post of source.

If we try to access a state post of a source which is present in the automaton as an initial/final state, yet does not have allocated space in the relation, an empty_post is returned. Hence, the function has no side effects (no allocation is performed and iterators remain valid).

inline const PostType &operator[](const State source) const¶
PostType &mutable_state_post(State source)

Get mutable (non-constant) reference to the state post of source.

The function allows modifying the state post. BEWARE, IT HAS A SIDE EFFECT. If we try to access a state post of a source which is present in the automaton as an initial/final state, yet does not have allocated space in the relation, a new state post for source will be allocated along with all state posts for all previous states. This in turn may cause that the entire post data structure is re-allocated. Iterators into the relation will get invalidated. The relation cannot see edits made through the reference, so the next query of the transition count recounts. The reference may be used for edits only until that query: num_of_transitions(), empty(), or any operation that may call them. Obtain the reference again after such a query.

Parameters:

source – Source state of a state post to access.

Returns:

State post of source.

Automaton¶

mata::AutomatonBase owns delta, initial and final together with the graph-only operations over them. It is parameterised by the transition relation and reads State, Target and key_arity off it, so the two cannot disagree. It is a base class rather than one instantiated directly, and its members are documented as part of Nondeterministic Finite automata and Nondeterministic Finite Transducers, which is where you will use them. The alias every automaton in the tree actually derives from, mata::Automaton, is in The shipped relation with the relation it is built on.

The structural base class shared by all automata in Mata.

mata::AutomatonBase holds the parts of an automaton that carry no language semantics. Every operation defined here is a pass over delta, initial and final, and is therefore meaningful for any transition relation satisfying mata::DeltaLike.

namespace mata

Main namespace including structs and algorithms for all automata.

In particular, this includes:

  1. Alphabets,

  2. Formula graphs and nodes,

  3. Mintermization,

  4. Closed sets.

template<DeltaLike D>
class AutomatonBase
#include <automaton.hh>

A class representing the structural part of an automaton.

Every operation defined here is a pass over delta, initial and final.

See also

mata::DeltaLike for what D must provide.

Note

A data-owning mixin, not a polymorphic base: it owns delta, initial and final, and has no virtual functions. The members that need their most-derived type take an explicit object parameter (deducing this) instead.

Note

D needs no keys: every operation here follows successors only, so the relation may be a plain graph.

Note

The largest State is reserved as “no state”, for initial and final as much as for delta: the algorithms count states in State and use the largest one as a marker.

Template Parameters:

D – The transition relation. Every other type is read off D rather than passed alongside it, so the two cannot disagree.

template<AutomatonWithRuns Self>
bool is_lang_empty(typename Self::Run *cex) const

Is the accepted language (or relation) empty, with a counter-example?

Note

Only for an automaton that has runs: the run type comes from Self.

Note

Unifying the two searches – having the Tarjan search emit a witness on demand – would save a traversal on the counter-example path, which is_included() and is_universal() take whenever the caller wants one. It would also stop the witness being shortest, and callers do depend on which one comes back (see the exact-word check in the “mata::nfa::Nfa::get_word()” tests). Worth doing only together with a decision about that.

Parameters:

cex – [out] Counter-example run, filled when an accepting path exists. With nullptr, none is built.

Returns:

true iff no accepting path exists.

bool is_acyclic() const

Is the part of the automaton graph reachable from the initial states acyclic?

A cycle no initial state reaches does not count.

Returns:

true iff no cycle is reachable from an initial state.

bool has_no_accepting_path() const

Is no final state reachable from any initial state?

A plain breadth-first search over a visited bit vector that stops at the first final state. This is a pure graph property; whether it coincides with the emptiness of the accepted language (or relation) is a fact about the concrete automaton class.

Returns:

true <-> no accepting path exists.

template<typename Self>
bool is_identical(const Self &other) const

Check if this is structuralry identical to other.

Compares only delta, initial and final. This is exact structural equality, including state numbering (so even stronger than isomorphism), essentially only useful for testing purposes.

Note

Templated on Self (deducing this) so that only same-type comparisons compile.

Parameters:

other – [in] The other automaton to compare with.

Returns:

true iff the structural parts of this and other are identical.

template<typename Self>
Self &trim(StateRenaming *state_renaming = nullptr)

Remove unreachable and non-terminating states in-place.

Remaining states are renumbered densely in ascending order.

Note

A state is reachable when the state is the endpoint of a path starting from an initial state. A state is terminating when the state is the starting point of a path ending in a final state.

Note

Reached only through a leaf’s own one-line trim(), on *this, so an lvalue Self suffices here.

Parameters:

state_renaming – [out] Mapping of trimmed states to new states.

Returns:

this after trimming.

The shipped relation¶

Everything above is generic. This is the one instantiation the library ships — mata::Delta and the aliases around it, depth 2, symbols keying states — kept out of core/ so that “does core name a concrete relation?” has an answer, and the answer is no.

The depth-2 relation (state, symbol, StateSet) shipped with the library, and automata built on it.

struct PostWorkspace¶
#include <relation.hh>

Reusable buffers of Delta::post() and Delta::epsilon_closure(), so that a loop of steps allocates once.

Keys on the transitions

Which outermost keys are in use. They ask nothing of a key beyond the ordering the posts already rely on, so a relation keyed by an interval or a weight has them too; what those keys stand for is that relation’s business. Protected for the same reason: a relation re-exports the ones it wants under the names that fit its keys, with a using-declaration or a forwarder. mata::Delta does the latter, as symbols, since for the shipped relation a key is one.

The three variants indexed by the key’s value need an unsigned integer for it.

doxygenfile does not render concept declarations, so each one is named explicitly below.

template<typename D>
concept DeltaLike¶
#include <concepts.hh>

A concept for a transition relation an mata::AutomatonBase can be built on.

Exactly what the structural algorithms use: a graph over states, with no keys and no post. A relation built from mata::posts::Post satisfies it, but so does a plain adjacency list.

Note

One contract, deliberately whole so the errors are reported immediately, rather then at the calls inside functions that need them.

Note

The largest State is reserved as “no state”: a relation never holds it as a state, so it has at most that many states.

Note

The automaton’s states can outnumber the relation’s: an initial or final state may have no transitions stored. The traversal members (for_each_successor(), successor_cursor(), has_self_loop()) are called for every state of the automaton, and have to treat such a state as one without transitions, rather than reject it.

template<typename C, typename Target>
concept SuccessorCursorLike¶
#include <concepts.hh>

A concept for a cursor over the targets of one state, as Tarjan’s SCC traversal walks it.

The traversal keeps one iterator per state, to resume it after visiting a successor. So the iterator has to be default-constructible and copyable, yield the targets, and end at std::default_sentinel.

Note

The traversal keeps only the iterator, not the cursor it came from, which is a temporary. So the iterator has to stay valid after the cursor is destroyed, for as long as the relation is not modified: it has to point into the relation, not into the cursor.

template<typename A>
concept AutomatonWithRuns¶
#include <concepts.hh>

A concept for an automaton that can report its runs.

template<typename A>
concept ExtensibleAlphabet¶
#include <concepts.hh>

A concept for an alphabet that can be extended with symbols it has not seen.

Only some alphabets can: a fixed EnumAlphabet cannot grow, an OnTheFlyAlphabet can. mata::posts::DeltaBase::add_keys_to() needs the growing kind.

The symbol type is the alphabet’s own Symbol alias, which mata::Alphabet supplies. An alphabet that is not mata’s declares one too: it has to name its members the way this concept does anyway, so it is written for mata and has nothing to adapt from outside.

template<typename T>
concept Printable¶
#include <concepts.hh>

A concept for a value with a printed form.

A user type gets one by specialising std::formatter. It is checked as const, the way it is printed.

See also

mata::utils::format_or_unprintable.

Post vocabulary¶

What mata::posts::DeltaBase and the visits need of a chain of posts, including where a post’s reserved keys begin. A relation built some other way does not need them.

template<typename R>

#include <concepts.hh>

A concept for a reserved-key convention (see mata::ReservedKeys).

template<typename L>
concept SortedWithReservedKeys¶
#include <concepts.hh>

A concept for a post ordered by key, whose reserved keys are described over that same key.

Three requirements:

  • the post declares sorted_by_key, so a lookup may binary-search it and mata::posts::Post::first_epsilon_it() may scan back from its end

  • it names a Reserved satisfying ReservedKeysLike;

  • that Reserved is over the post’s own Key.

template<typename L>
concept PostLike¶
#include <concepts.hh>

A concept for a post, a range of entries that can be iterated, updated, and queried.

Note

Moving a post must leave its entries where they are, as moving a std::vector does, and must not throw. A relation moves its posts whenever it grows, and the targets passed to its add() may be borrowed from one of them. A std::vector that grows moves its elements only if that cannot throw, and copies them otherwise, which would leave such borrowed targets dangling.
